title: Skills are new features: Building Skill-Centric Harness — Yogendra Miraje, FactSet
talk_summary: Yogendra Miraje describes treating agent 'skills' (SKILL.md files with name/description front matter and progressive disclosure) as the new product features, and argues engineers should build the harness that runs them. He gives concrete mechanics: a skill registry concatenated into the system prompt by name+description only, description-as-routing-signal, evals per model upgrade, and governance (admission, ownership, boundaries, lifecycle, coherence) borrowed from code review.

takeaways.what_they_do: Maintain a registry of skills (name, description, path) and inject only name+description+path into the system prompt; the agent reads the full skill body via a file-read tool only when it decides the skill applies.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we are only using the name and description path in in this system prompt and not the skill body and that's what what they call about is progressive disclosure

takeaways.what_they_do: Write skill descriptions around the user/task trigger words rather than describing the skill, and keep descriptions distinct so the model picks the right one; stale or overlapping descriptions cause skills to not fire.
takeaways.evidence_quote: descriptions are really the routing signals ... keep your descriptions aligned to the user request and not about the skill itself

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat skills as contracts versioned to a model; rerun skill evals on every model upgrade because a new model can silently stop obeying instructions (e.g. attending only to the start of the skill).
takeaways.evidence_quote: skills are really the contracts versioned to a model ... whenever you're upgrading a model, make sure to rerun uh your eval

takeaways.technique: Put critical instructions early; cut by user intent not data model
takeaways.what_they_do: After a model upgrade failed because critical instructions sat at the end of the skill, they moved key instructions to the top. They also refactored skills around real user-intent workflows rather than data-model slices.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this like new model was very focusing on beginning of the skill and we had very critical instruction at the end of the skill

takeaways.technique: Skill library governance modeled on code review
takeaways.what_they_do: Apply five governance axes to the skill library: admission (should this be a new skill or extend one), ownership (named maintainers like CODEOWNERS), boundaries (allow-listed tools per skill), lifecycle (semver, deprecation, changelog), coherence (periodic audits), with automated gates plus human-in-the-loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we build automated get for the registries with human in the loop. And this is very analog log to how we do the PR review process

takeaways.technique: Shortlist skills before prompt injection at scale
takeaways.what_they_do: Shoving all skills into the system prompt works up to ~10; beyond that use embedding similarity or a small model to shortlist skills, and at hundreds add hierarchy plus metadata filters.
takeaways.evidence_quote: When you have like more than 10 skill, maybe that's like a good point to think start thinking about, you know, how can you shortlist the skills
takeaways.numbers: ~10 skills as the threshold where full injection stops working
